questions.stem: To a historian of the modern world, an archive is best described as:
options: an organised collection of records kept for their long-term value as evidence
a published narrative history written by experts using a range of sources
a museum display that interprets past events for visitors and visiting school groups
a database of historians' interpretations of particular events and people
questions.explanation: Archives hold original records such as government files, letters, diaries, photographs and business papers, kept because they are evidence of past activity. A published history or museum display interprets that evidence; it is not the archive itself.

questions.stem: The National Archives of Australia has digitised the service records of First World War personnel. Which is the most significant benefit of this for historical research?
options: Anyone can search and read the records online, widening who can study the war
Digitised copies are more reliable than the paper files they were scanned from
Historians no longer need to consider who created the records or for what purpose
The records now include the soldiers' own views, which the originals left out
questions.explanation: Digitisation greatly widens access: family historians, students and researchers anywhere can use the files. A scan is only as reliable as the original record, and historians must still ask who created a record and why.

questions.stem: A historian notes that a digitised newspaper collection is searchable by keyword, but that the computer-read text of many old pages contains errors. What problem does this create?
options: Keyword searching removes any need to read the articles in the context of the whole page
A keyword search may miss relevant articles, so results can seem more complete than they are
The scanned page images cannot be trusted, so the original papers must always be consulted
Newspapers become primary sources only once they have been digitised and indexed online
questions.explanation: Errors in machine-read text mean a search can silently miss articles, so a researcher may wrongly think a topic was rarely reported. The page image itself is still a faithful copy, and reading articles in context remains essential.

questions.stem: Oral history is best defined as:
options: historians' lectures about the past recorded for students and the general public
recorded interviews with people about their own memories and experiences of the past
the stories passed down within families that have never been written down or checked
speeches made by political leaders that were broadcast live on radio or television
questions.explanation: Oral history records people speaking about what they lived through, usually in a structured interview. It is valuable for groups who left few written records, though memory can change over time.

questions.stem: Which is the main strength of oral history for investigating the experiences of factory workers in the 1950s?
options: It records perspectives of ordinary people that official documents often left out
It gives exact dates and figures that are more accurate than written company records
It is free from bias because the speakers are describing their own experiences
It replaces the need to corroborate evidence because the witnesses were present
questions.explanation: Oral history captures everyday experiences, feelings and perspectives that rarely appear in official records. Memory is weaker on exact dates and figures, and personal accounts are still shaped by hindsight and perspective, so they need corroboration.

questions.stem: Interviewed in 1990, a veteran describes a battle from 1944 in vivid detail, including a conversation he says he overheard between two generals. What should a historian be most cautious about?
options: Later reading, retelling and hindsight may have reshaped what he remembers he witnessed
Veterans are always unreliable because they wish to glorify their own role in war
Oral evidence cannot be used for events that happened more than ten years earlier
A personal account of a battle has no value unless the speaker was an officer
questions.explanation: Memories can absorb details from later books, films and retellings, and an overheard conversation between senior officers is the kind of detail that should be checked. That does not make all veterans unreliable; it means testing the account against other evidence.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a scientific technique contributing to the investigation of modern history?
options: DNA testing to identify the remains of soldiers recovered from wartime mass graves
reading a soldier's diary to learn about conditions in the trenches in 1916
comparing two historians' accounts of the causes of the First World War
interviewing descendants about the family stories of a soldier's wartime service
questions.explanation: DNA analysis compares genetic material from remains with samples from living relatives. The other methods are valuable, but they are documentary or oral methods, not scientific techniques.

questions.stem: After research by an amateur historian, mass graves of soldiers killed at Fromelles in 1916 were confirmed at Pheasant Wood in 2008. How was the identification of many of the 250 recovered soldiers achieved?
options: Archaeological recovery combined with DNA matching against samples from relatives
Matching the soldiers' faces to photographs held by the Australian War Memorial
Reading names stamped on the soldiers' rifles and helmets found in the graves
Using German burial registers that listed each soldier by name and grave position
questions.explanation: Oxford Archaeology recovered the remains in 2009, and an identification board combined archaeological, anthropological and historical evidence with DNA from relatives. Many soldiers have been named this way, showing how science can recover individual stories.

questions.stem: A historian uses dated building plans, photographs from different decades and layers of debris to work out when each part of a former migrant hostel was built and altered. This is an example of:
options: testing the authenticity of a single source by scientific dating
reconstructing a site's chronology using several types of evidence
constructing an official history of a site for government purposes
commemorating a site through a memorial and an annual ceremony
questions.explanation: Reconstructing site chronology means establishing the sequence of building, use and change at a place by combining documents, images and physical evidence. Commemoration and official histories are about how the past is presented, not how it is reconstructed.

questions.stem: Why do historians value visiting and studying a historic site, such as a preserved battlefield or a former prison, in addition to written records?
options: Sites present a single agreed interpretation, so they avoid the problem of bias entirely
Studying a site removes the need to consult archives for dates and names
The physical setting can reveal conditions and distances that documents do not convey
Sites are unchanged since the events, so they are more reliable than written records
questions.explanation: A site can show scale, terrain, living conditions and spatial relationships that help explain events. But most sites have been altered, restored or interpreted since, so they too must be read critically alongside documents.

questions.stem: Corroboration means:
options: accepting a source because it was written at the time of the event
rejecting a source because its author had a clear point of view
summarising a source in a historian's own words for an essay
checking a piece of evidence against other independent sources
questions.explanation: Historians corroborate by testing whether independent sources agree. A source written at the time can still be wrong, and a biased source can still be useful evidence.

questions.stem: A historian hypothesises that a city's strikes in 1917 were caused mainly by food shortages. Which approach best tests this hypothesis?
options: Accepting the explanation given in the government's official report on the strikes
Choosing only sources that mention food so the argument stays clearly focused
Comparing strike dates with price records, police reports and workers' accounts
Finding one striker's memoir that names food shortages as the main grievance
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is tested by seeing whether several independent kinds of evidence support it, and by looking for evidence against it. Selecting only supporting sources, or relying on one account, would not test it at all.

questions.stem: In historical inquiry, a source's authenticity refers to whether it:
options: was written by an eyewitness who was present when the events took place
has been published by a reputable historian or a government archive
is genuinely what it claims to be, made by the stated author at the stated time
gives an accurate and balanced account of the events and people that it describes
questions.explanation: Authenticity asks whether a source is genuine rather than a forgery or misattribution. Reliability is a separate question: an authentic source can still be inaccurate or one-sided.

questions.stem: In 1983 the German magazine Stern published extracts from what it claimed were Adolf Hitler's diaries. How was the fraud exposed?
options: A rival magazine bought the originals and found pages copied from Mein Kampf
Forensic tests found materials in the paper and binding made after the war
Hitler's former secretaries swore that he had never kept a personal diary
Historians found that the diaries contradicted every published speech of Hitler
questions.explanation: Tests by German federal experts found materials in the diaries that were not produced until after 1945. The forger, Konrad Kujau, was later jailed. The case is a classic lesson in testing authenticity scientifically, not just by content.

questions.stem: The historian Hugh Trevor-Roper at first declared the 'Hitler Diaries' genuine in 1983 but soon withdrew his view. Which lesson does this case best teach about evaluating sources?
options: Sources about famous leaders are more likely to be forged than other sources
Only scientists, not historians, are qualified to judge whether a source is genuine
Expert judgement of content is not enough without scientific and provenance checks
Historians should never give a view on a source until decades after it is found
questions.explanation: Trevor-Roper was impressed by the volume and apparent detail of the material, but he was given little time and the physical testing had not been done. The lesson is that content, provenance and scientific analysis must all be checked; historians still play a key role.

questions.stem: A source's reliability refers mainly to:
options: how old the source is compared with the events it describes
whether the source is a written document rather than an image
how far it can be trusted as accurate evidence for a particular inquiry
whether it was produced by the person and at the time that it claims
questions.explanation: Reliability concerns how trustworthy a source is for the question being asked, considering its author, purpose, audience and accuracy. Whether a source is genuine is a question of authenticity.

questions.stem: A propaganda poster from 1915 shows enemy soldiers as monsters. A student says it is useless because it is biased. Which response is most accurate?
options: It is unreliable about the enemy but useful evidence of wartime attitudes and aims
It is reliable because it was produced at the time by the government of the day
It is useless for any inquiry because propaganda is designed to deceive its audience
It becomes reliable once a second poster with the same message has been found
questions.explanation: Usefulness depends on the question. A biased source can be excellent evidence of the beliefs, fears and methods of those who made it. Finding another poster with the same message corroborates the propaganda, not the claim about the enemy.

questions.stem: Why is understanding historical context important when interpreting a source?
options: A source should only be interpreted using the values of the present day
Context matters only for sources written in a language other than English
Words and images can carry meanings at the time that differ from their meaning today
Context tells the historian whether the source is authentic or a later forgery
questions.explanation: Knowing the circumstances, audience and conventions of the time stops historians from misreading a source through present-day assumptions. Context can help with authenticity, but its main role is accurate interpretation.

questions.stem: A 1940 newspaper article praises a dictator's foreign policy. Which piece of context would most change a historian's reading of it?
options: The journalist had travelled widely before writing the article
The article was written in the evening edition rather than the morning
The paper was published under strict state censorship at the time
The article was later reprinted in a collection of wartime documents
questions.explanation: If the press was censored, praise may reflect what was permitted rather than the writer's or public's views. The other details do little to change what the article can tell us.

questions.stem: David Irving sued the historian Deborah Lipstadt for libel in a London court after she described him as a Holocaust denier. What was the outcome of the case, decided in 2000?
options: Irving lost; the judge found he had deliberately distorted historical evidence
Irving won, but the damages were small because the judge found both sides at fault
The case was dropped before trial when Lipstadt withdrew and apologised
The court refused to hear it because historical questions cannot be tried
questions.explanation: Justice Gray ruled for Lipstadt and her publisher, finding that Irving had misrepresented and manipulated evidence for ideological reasons. The case showed how interpretations can be tested against the evidence and how denial differs from legitimate debate.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes legitimate historical debate from denial of the past?
options: Debate concerns causes only; denial concerns whether particular events happened
Debate accepts the official version of events; denial questions it in any way
Debate weighs all the evidence; denial rejects or distorts evidence to fit a set conclusion
Debate is carried out by academics; denial is any view put forward by non-historians
questions.explanation: Historians legitimately disagree about causes, significance and meaning, but they argue from the evidence and revise views when it changes. Denial starts from a conclusion and ignores or manipulates evidence. Questioning official versions is a normal part of history.

questions.stem: In 1943 Nazi Germany announced the discovery of mass graves of Polish officers at Katyn. For decades the Soviet Union blamed Germany. Which development settled the question?
options: Polish historians in the 1950s published Soviet documents blaming Germany
Forensic testing in the 1960s proved the graves dated from the German invasion
In 1990 the Soviet government admitted that its NKVD had carried out the killings
A 1946 international court found Germany responsible for it at the Nuremberg trials
questions.explanation: Under Gorbachev, the Soviet Union admitted in 1990 that the NKVD carried out the Katyn massacre of 1940, and documents were later released. Katyn shows how political power can shape an official version of the past until evidence becomes available.

questions.stem: 'History from below' is an approach that focuses on:
options: the archaeology of buried sites, studied by excavating layers of soil
the lives and actions of ordinary people rather than leaders and elites
the decisions of political leaders as seen through their private papers
the history of underground movements such as resistance and spy networks
questions.explanation: History from below, associated with historians such as E. P. Thompson, studies workers, peasants, women and other groups often absent from traditional political history.

questions.stem: A book examines how ideas about masculinity and femininity shaped work, politics and family life in Britain during the Second World War. This is best described as:
options: diplomatic history
gender history
military history
economic history
questions.explanation: Gender history studies how ideas about men's and women's roles shaped, and were shaped by, events. A military history would focus on campaigns and forces; a diplomatic history on relations between states.

questions.stem: An official history is best described as a history that is:
options: produced by a museum to accompany an exhibition for the general public
commissioned or sponsored by a government or institution, often with access to its records
written by a professional historian and published by a university press for academics
based entirely on oral interviews with eyewitnesses collected after the events
questions.explanation: Official histories are sponsored by governments, armed forces or institutions, which often give access to their records. Examples include C. E. W. Bean's official history of Australia in the First World War. Their sponsorship raises questions about independence.

questions.stem: C. E. W. Bean edited the Official History of Australia in the War of 1914-1918. Which feature of his approach is most often noted?
options: He gave close attention to the experiences of ordinary soldiers in battle
He relied entirely on British army records and ignored Australian sources
He wrote the whole history in a single volume within a year of the war's end
He argued that Australia should not have taken part in the war at all
questions.explanation: Bean, who had been at Gallipoli and on the Western Front as a war correspondent, wrote in detail about individual soldiers and small units. Historians since have also asked how his work helped build the Anzac legend.

questions.stem: Two historians studying the same strike use the same records. One stresses the workers' grievances; the other stresses the role of union organisers. Which concept best explains why their accounts differ?
options: Corroboration, because only one historian checked other sources
Commemoration, because each wished to honour a different group
Interpretation, shaped by each historian's questions and perspective
Authenticity, because one of the two must have relied on forged records
questions.explanation: Historians select, emphasise and explain evidence differently depending on their questions, assumptions and perspective, so the same evidence can support different interpretations. Nothing suggests the records are forged.

questions.stem: Which is an example of omission in the construction of a historical account?
options: A history that explains its choice of sources in an introduction
A history of a colonial town that mentions only its settlers and ignores the labourers it relied on
A history that quotes a primary source at length and then analyses its meaning
A history that compares the views of several historians on the same question
questions.explanation: Omission means leaving out people, events or evidence, which can distort an account even if everything included is accurate. Explaining source choices and comparing views are signs of careful method.

questions.stem: A history of the industrial revolution devotes ten chapters to inventors and factory owners and one paragraph to child workers. Which construction problem does this best illustrate?
options: Corroboration, as the historian has not checked sources against each other
Emphasis, as some groups are given far more weight than others
Anachronism, as the historian has judged the past by modern values
Authenticity, as the sources about child workers may be forgeries
questions.explanation: Emphasis concerns how much weight an account gives to different people and factors. It shapes readers' understanding of what mattered, even when nothing is factually wrong.

questions.stem: Why do historians often say that each generation rewrites history?
options: Governments require history to be rewritten after every change of leader
The facts of past events change as time passes and as living memories fade
New evidence, questions and concerns lead historians to reinterpret the past
Earlier histories are usually found to be based on forged documents
questions.explanation: The events themselves do not change, but historians ask new questions, use new methods and find new evidence, such as opened archives. Government rewriting happens in some states, but it is not why historiography develops.

questions.stem: Historians of the Cold War are often grouped as orthodox, revisionist and post-revisionist. A post-revisionist account would most likely argue that:
options: the USA alone was responsible because of its drive for economic markets
neither superpower's actions mattered because the conflict was inevitable
both superpowers' fears and misperceptions contributed to the conflict
the Soviet Union alone was responsible because of its expansionist ideology
questions.explanation: Post-revisionists, such as John Lewis Gaddis in his earlier work, moved beyond blaming one side and stressed mutual suspicion, security fears and misperception. Orthodox accounts blamed the Soviet Union; revisionist accounts emphasised American policy.

questions.stem: Public history refers to history that is:
options: written only about governments and public officials, not private lives
open to anyone at all to edit, such as online encyclopaedia entries
presented to general audiences through museums, sites, media and memorials
paid for entirely from public taxes rather than by private universities
questions.explanation: Public history includes museums, heritage sites, documentaries, monuments and anniversaries that present the past to the wider community. It reaches far more people than academic history.

questions.stem: In 1995 the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum planned an exhibition around the Enola Gay, the aircraft that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima. What happened?
options: It was cancelled because historians agreed the decision to use the bomb was not debated
After protests from veterans' groups and politicians it was cut back to a much smaller display
It opened as planned, with sections on Japanese casualties and the decision to use the bomb
It was moved to Japan after American museums refused to show the aircraft at all
questions.explanation: Critics said the planned script gave too much weight to Japanese suffering and to doubts about the bombing. The museum dropped it and showed the fuselage with limited interpretation, and the director resigned. It shows political influence on public representations of the past.

questions.stem: Anzac Day on 25 April marks the anniversary of:
options: the armistice that ended fighting on the Western Front in 1918
the first major battle fought by the Australian Imperial Force in France
the departure of the first Australian troop convoy from Albany
the landing of Australian and New Zealand troops at Gallipoli in 1915
questions.explanation: Anzac Day commemorates the Gallipoli landing on 25 April 1915 and has broadened to honour all Australians and New Zealanders who served. Remembrance Day on 11 November marks the 1918 armistice.

questions.stem: After 1991, many statues of Lenin in former Soviet republics were removed. A historian would most likely use this to show that:
options: Lenin's historical significance was reassessed only by professional historians
monuments cannot be studied as historical sources once they are removed
commemoration reflects the political values of the present, not only the past
the removed statues had been inaccurate likenesses of Lenin and were replaced
questions.explanation: Monuments express what a regime or community wants to honour, so when power and values change, commemoration changes too. Their erection and removal are themselves valuable evidence for historians.

questions.stem: A film about a wartime battle invents a romance and merges several real officers into one hero. Which is the most useful critical question for a historian to ask about it?
options: Did the film earn enough at the box office to influence public opinion widely?
Were the actors chosen to look as much as possible like the people they portray?
Was the film made using the same type of equipment as films of the war period?
What has been changed or added for drama, and how does it shape viewers' understanding?
questions.explanation: Critical analysis of a representation asks what is accurate, what has been invented or simplified, why, and with what effect on the audience's view of the past. Box office figures and casting are side issues.

questions.stem: Which example best shows political influence on the commemoration of the past?
options: A government funds a national memorial and chooses which events its displays will honour
A family places a plaque at the house where a relative was born a century earlier
A historian publishes a peer-reviewed article reinterpreting a battle's significance
A local museum displays a set of donated letters in the order in which they were written
questions.explanation: When governments fund and shape memorials, anniversaries and museum displays, they decide what is remembered and how, which can serve present political aims. The other examples are private or scholarly acts.
